notes: Long copyright trial on indirect copying of sign-frame drawings; outcome and legal analysis are clear throughout.

enrichment.short_title: Copyright in aluminium sign-frame drawing: indirect copying rejected
key_facts: Tom Scott claimed copyright in a 1976 scheme drawing for extruded aluminium sign frames with demountable cleat-locating pips.
Universal Components added pips to its Panatrim sign-frame range in 1992 after Ultraframe entered the market.
Scott alleged indirect copying via GAP 500 and Ultraframe, though he owned copyright in the 1976 drawing but not GAP 500.
Indalex draftsman Martin Ford produced Panatrim 5 and Panatrim Major profiles with pips from pre-existing Panatrim dies and JM 1054.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a copyright infringement claim in the Chancery Division after a preliminary issue on ownership of GAP 500.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the 1976 drawing was an original artistic work but Universal Components independently designed its pip profiles and did not copy it.
enrichment.ratio: Copyright protects the visual expression of an artistic work, not a general technical idea such as incorporating commonplace cleat-locating pips; similarities arising from shared design constraints and independent draughtsmanship do not establish indirect copying, and inspiration from a competitor's commercial success is not infringement.
legal_issues: Whether the 1976 drawing was an original artistic work entitled to copyright
Whether Universal Components indirectly copied the 1976 drawing through GAP 500 or Ultraframe
Whether verbal instructions to a designer could constitute indirect reproduction
Whether copyright could be carried forward through intermediate drawings under LA Gear

LA Gear Inc v Hi-Tec Sports plc [1992] FSR 121
Solar Thomson Engineering Co Ltd v Barton [1977] RPC 537
British Leyland Motor Corporation Ltd v Armstrong Patents Co Ltd [1986] AC 577
Francis Day & Hunter Ltd v Bron [1963] Ch 587

notes: Short written appeal on excluded subject matter; Deputy Director's reasoning adopted without difficulty.

enrichment.short_title: Advent calendar patent excluded as presentation of information
key_facts: Stephen Townsend, a patent agent, appealed refusal of GB0301172.3 for an advent calendar with extra door markings for multiple users.
Claim 1 required at least one door to bear an additional indicium identifying which user should open it.
The examiner and Deputy Director held the invention excluded as presentation of information.
The appeal was dealt with in writing without an oral hearing to save costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Patents Court from a Comptroller decision refusing a patent application under section 18(3).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 1(2)(d) of the Patents Act 1977 excludes inventions consisting of the presentation of information in its natural meaning, including providing information by marking calendar doors for particular users; the exclusion is not limited to how information is expressed.
legal_issues: Whether marking advent calendar doors with user-specific indicia is excluded subject matter
Whether presentation of information means expression rather than provision of information
Whether Pepper v Hart or EPC language aids construction of section 1(2)(d)

notes: First High Court appeal from the Care Standards Tribunal; jurisdiction point resolved for Ofsted but tribunal decision quashed on defective conditions and reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Childminder emergency cancellation: tribunal decision quashed

statutes_considered.title: Day Care and Child Minding (National Standards) (England) Regulations 2003

key_facts: Mrs Spicer, a registered childminder since 1989, had her registration cancelled under section 79K after Ofsted found sixteen children at her home on 11 March 2003.
The Care Standards Tribunal allowed her appeal, reinstated registration with reduced child numbers, and made recommendations on training and records.
Ofsted appealed on whether the tribunal could rely on post-magistrates' order events and whether imposed conditions were valid.
The tribunal found grounds for the emergency order existed but concluded future significant harm was unlikely with tighter limits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on points of law from a Care Standards Tribunal decision reinstating a childminder's registration after an emergency cancellation order.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision quashed and remitted to a differently constituted tribunal; Chief Inspector succeeded on the jurisdiction to consider post-order evidence but failed on the outcome; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: On a true rehearing under section 79M, the Care Standards Tribunal may consider evidence and circumstances arising after a justice's section 79K order, including an appellant's admissions and changed circumstances; but registration conditions must be clear and mandatory, not dependent on consent, and central reasoning must be intelligible.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal could consider matters after the magistrates' emergency order
Whether the tribunal acted as first-instance decision maker rather than appellate body
Whether a condition subject to the childminder's consent was valid
Whether recommendations were improperly mandatory or inadequately reasoned
index_terms: Lyons v East Sussex County Council
linked_authorities: Lyons v East Sussex County Council (1988) 86 LGR 369
C v Ofsted [2002] 0087EY

notes: Renewed permission application on Article 6 reasons; brief oral judgment with clear refusal.

enrichment.short_title: NNDR liability order: no Article 6 breach for absent hearing
key_facts: Mr Mathialagen sought judicial review of Camberwell Green Magistrates' liability orders for national non-domestic rates on former solicitor's premises.
After several adjournments the magistrates heard the case in his absence on 19 September 2003 and granted liability orders.
His wife, acting pro bono, attended on 16 September when the court was closed due to flooding, mistaking the hearing date.
Beatson J refused permission; the renewed application relied on failure to give reasons rather than unfair absence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review of magistrates' NNDR liability orders.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; no arguable breach of Article 6 where the claimant and his representatives did not attend and no contrary submissions were made.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6 does not require detailed reasons where a ratepayer fails to attend after repeated adjournments and warning that the case would proceed in absence, and the magistrate grants liability on an undisputed basis without live argument to address.
legal_issues: Whether the magistrates' decision should be quashed for proceeding in absence
Whether failure to give reasons breached Article 6(1)
Whether advisor mistake and court closure on the wrong date engaged unfair procedure
linked_authorities: English v Emery Reimbold and Strick Ltd [2002] 1 WLR 385
Torija v Spain (1994) 19 EHRR 553
Al Nedawi [1991] ACH 36

notes: Category A review challenge with detailed parole-policy discussion; all four grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Category A prisoner: downgrading judicial review refused
key_facts: Mr Roberts is serving concurrent life sentences for a 1991 double murder he denies committing.
The Category A Review Team decided in May 2003 that he should remain category A despite satisfactory prison behaviour.
The team relied on unaddressed risk factors including potential extreme violence and refusal to do offence-focused courses while denying guilt.
Roberts challenged reliance on denial, weight given to good behaviour, parole progression effects, and escape-potential assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of a Category A Review Team decision refusing downgrading to category B.
enrichment.ratio: Denial of guilt is not itself a bar to recategorisation but may make it practically difficult to demonstrate diminished risk without offence-focused work; the review team need not anticipate future Parole Board views, and a two-stage exceptional-circumstances approach to escape potential can be lawful where category A aims to make escape impossible.
legal_issues: Whether denial of guilt improperly prevented category B downgrading
Whether insufficient weight was given to good custodial behaviour and R&R programme participation
Whether parole progression implications must be considered before any Parole Board decision
Whether escape potential was wrongly excluded unless exceptional circumstances existed

R (Williams) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] EWCA Civ 498
R v Parole Board ex p Oyston (1 March 2000)

notes: Neighbour dispute on adverse possession and proprietary estoppel; appeal and cross-appeal both dismissed with clear fact/law analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Neighbour boundary: adverse possession upheld, estoppel rejected
key_facts: Miss Pleming claimed half a shared concrete path between Nos 1 and 4 Cuba Cottages in Maidenhead against neighbours the Hamptons.
The Hamptons enclosed the path within their garden with hedge, fence, shed and oil tank, stopping its use as a right of way.
The county court judge found adverse possession of the eastern half of the path and dismissed both claim and counterclaim.
Mrs Margaret Pleming had promised a 2-foot driveway strip in a February 2002 letter after her daughter had become registered owner.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from Slough County Court adverse possession and proprietary estoppel proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; adverse possession upheld and no proprietary estoppel or constructive trust over the promised strip.
enrichment.ratio: Exclusive garden use of a path no longer used as a granted right of way can establish factual possession and intention to possess for adverse possession under Pye v Graham; a promise by a non-owner without authority cannot bind the registered proprietor, and failure to cooperate with building works defeats estoppel relief.
legal_issues: Whether use of the path was referable to an easement or adverse possession
Whether the Hamptons had factual possession and intention to possess
Whether full cooperation under the February 2002 letter gave rise to proprietary estoppel
Whether the registered owner was bound by her mother's promise
linked_authorities: JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2003] 1 AC 419
Powell v McFarlane [1977] 38 P&CR 452
Yaxley v Gotts [2000] Ch 162
Gillett v Holt [2001] Ch 210

notes: Emotive WWII enemy-property scheme case; multiple grounds rejected though judge expressed sympathy on interest point.

enrichment.short_title: WWII enemy property: no uplift under 1999 compensation scheme
key_facts: Yakob Kaplan claimed inflation uplift under the 1999 Enemy Property Payments Scheme for bank deposits confiscated in WWII.
Moses Kaplan and Boris Baksht, Estonian Jewish businessmen, deposited funds in London before Soviet deportation to Siberia in June 1941.
Nominal sums were repaid in 1971 under the Baltic States Scheme; company deposits were partially recognised in 2002.
The adjudicator rejected claims as not Nazi persecution and as fully settled in 1971 without interest or revaluation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an Enemy Property Claims Assessment Panel adjudicator's dismissal of appeals for inflation uplift on previously repaid confiscated deposits.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Presentation of information and executive compensation schemes are not justiciable on interest or uplift where the Baltic States Scheme paid nominal amounts only; Soviet deportation of bourgeois businessmen was not Nazi persecution by a relevant enemy state, and Bank voor Handel prevents possessory rights under Article 1 Protocol 1 for confiscated wartime property.
legal_issues: Whether 1971 repayments left claims open for interest or inflation uplift
Whether Soviet deportation constituted Nazi persecution under the EPPS criteria
Whether Germany or the USSR was the relevant enemy state
Whether section 7 of the 1939 Act or Article 1 Protocol 1 required additional compensation
linked_authorities: Bank Voor Handel en Scheepvaart N.V. v Administrator of Hungarian Property [1954] AC 584
Wilson v Secretary of State for Trade and Industry [2003] UKHL 40

confidence.notes: Outcome clear on all grounds. Judge expressed sympathy on 'settled in full' construction but did not need final ruling given other findings.

notes: Very long commercial trial on Mongolian government guarantee; authority, primary liability and Holme v Brunskill discharge all resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Mongolian government guarantee discharged by rescheduling variations
key_facts: Marubeni Hong Kong sued the Mongolian Ministry of Finance on a May 1996 letter guaranteeing Buyan's deferred payment obligations for a cashmere plant.
Buyan defaulted on instalments under the DPS1 Contract and the parties entered into 1998 and 1999 rescheduling packages without Mongolia's consent.
Reschedulings altered payment terms, added contracts, changed security interests and collateral account arrangements.
Cresswell J held the Minister had cabinet authority to issue the guarantee but the claim failed on surety discharge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial after service out and jurisdiction challenge dismissed; claim on a sovereign guarantee letter.
enrichment.outcome: Claim failed; Mongolia discharged from liability under the rule in Holme v Brunskill because 1998 and 1999 reschedulings were prejudicial material variations.
enrichment.ratio: Unless a guarantee creates primary joint liability, a guarantor is discharged by substantial variations to the underlying transaction without consent; combined rescheduling changes to payment terms, additional obligations, security rights and collateral arrangements were prejudicial and would discharge a surety under Holme v Brunskill.
legal_issues: Whether the MMOF Letter created primary or secondary liability
Whether the Minister had authority under Mongolian law to issue the guarantee
Whether 1998 and 1999 reschedulings materially varied the guaranteed transaction
Whether Mongolia was immune from suit and validly served
linked_authorities: Holme v Brunskill (1878) 3 QBD 495
Marubeni Hong Kong and South China Ltd v Mongolian Government [2002] 2 All ER (Comm) 873

notes: Disciplinary penalty appeal with straightforward Wednesbury review; suspension and fines upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Hearing aid dispenser: disciplinary penalties upheld on appeal
key_facts: Mr Gill, managing director of Harley Street Hearing Aid Centre, pleaded guilty to four breaches of the Hearing Aid Code of Practice.
The company rebranded manufacturer models with its own logo and selected aids remotely rather than giving best client advice.
Clients did not receive manufacturer make/model information or manufacturer guarantees; Gill failed to respond to Council enquiries.
The Council imposed three months' suspension, fines totalling £18,000 and £25,000 costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal against penalties imposed by the Hearing Aid Council after guilty pleas to code breaches.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; suspension and financial penalties not interfered with; appellant ordered to pay £4,250 costs.
enrichment.ratio: A specialist professional council's choice of suspension and maximum fines for sustained code breaches involving client advice, product identification and failure to cooperate with the regulator will not be overturned unless plainly wrong; misunderstanding of registrar discussions does not fetter disciplinary discretion.
legal_issues: Whether three months' suspension was disproportionate given the basis of plea
Whether maximum fines were improper without guilty-plea credit
Whether the registrar had indicated suspension would not be imposed
Whether the Council acted inconsistently in wishing Gill to remain in practice

notes: Planning law section 288 appeal on seasonal occupancy conditions; Nicholson distinguished with thorough reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Seasonal occupancy breach: ten-year immunity for lawful development certificate
key_facts: The owner of 2 Seymour Bungalows, Woolacombe occupied a holiday bungalow continuously year-round from October 1992 in breach of a seasonal condition.
The condition limited occupation to 15 March to 15 November under a 1971 planning permission for five holiday bungalows.
North Devon District Council refused a lawful development certificate, treating each winter as a fresh breach resetting the ten-year period.
An inspector allowed the appeal; the council challenged under section 288.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's decision granting a lawful development certificate for breach of a seasonal occupancy condition.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; inspector's decision upheld; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 171B(3), continuous seasonal breaches of the same condition over ten years can acquire enforcement immunity even where non-compliance is impossible year-round; Nicholson is distinguishable and should not be applied mechanically to seasonal conditions, and an enforcement notice could have been issued each winter during the period.
legal_issues: Whether each winter breach of a seasonal condition is a separate breach resetting limitation
Whether immunity can ever accrue for breach of seasonal occupancy conditions
How Nicholson v Secretary of State and Rottenbury apply to seasonal conditions
Whether enforcement after seasonal breach ceases is precluded by section 187A
linked_authorities: Nicholson v Secretary of State for the Environment and Malvern District Council [1998] JPL 553
Secretary of State for the Environment v Holding and Thurrock Borough Council [2002] JPL 1278
North Devon District Council v Rottenbury [1998] EG CS 72
R (St Anselm Development Co Ltd) v First Secretary of State [2003] EWHC 1592 (Admin)
